Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

vignette: Mahmoud, a seventy-eight-year-old roofer from a small Midwestern town, began his workday each morning with the clang of his safety harness and the scent of fresh cedar. On a July afternoon in 1995, the routine took a dark turn. While applying a sealant to a roof that had recently suffered a storm-related leak, a sudden flare from a leaking pipe released a pungent plume of solvent vapor. Mahmoud inhaled the fumes without noticing, his vision clouded and his breathing labored. By the time he staggered back to the worksite and called for assistance, he was already unconscious. He awoke days later in the hospital, feverish, with a lingering metallic taste and an uneasy sense that something inside him had been irrevocably altered. The memory of that day is a strange mosaic. Mahmoud can not deliberately pull the images into focus; each attempt feels like turning a dial to a broken stop. Yet, whenever the scent of oil or the hiss of a leaking pipe rises, the memory bursts forth, uncontrolled and unbidden. At those moments the mind is flooded not with photographs but with a raw, unfiltered emotion-an ache that feels as if a part of him has been torn out. He describes these episodes as "a wave of panic that doesn't come with a picture." He has tried to rehearse the event, to write it down, but the words either fall short or vanish entirely. The emotional intensity comes through without the scaffolding of a coherent image. These memories ignite a sense of threat that is immediate and visceral. Mahmoud finds himself startled by the most modest touch: a colleague's hand on his shoulder, a passerby's brush of his arm on a street corner. The startle is sharp, the heart pounding, the body rigid, as if he has stepped back into the day of the chemical spill. Even in the quiet of his bedroom, he cannot relax; a simple thought of his own hands-his hands that have spent a lifetime building roofs-provokes a surge of anxiety. Sleep has become a distant memory itself; he drifts in and out of consciousness, the sound of distant sirens or the hiss of a leaking pipe echoing in his mind, preventing any restful night. The triggers that flood Mahmoud's life are not limited to the physical sensations of the work site. He is surrounded by children on most days; his eldest son, a high school teacher, brings his four children home on weekends, the boys laughing as they play in his backyard. The sight of these children, so close to the places where Mahmoud once fought the toxic vapor, is enough to stir the memories again. News reports about a new chemical spill in a neighboring state, with graphic footage of emergency crews, also trigger a cascade of panic. Even acquaintances who casually mention "the incident" on the radio or in conversation send Mahmoud spiraling into that same unblinking terror. The cycle is relentless. When a child's laughter rings through the house, Mahmoud's mind immediately conjures the choking air, and the memory floods back. The memory, in turn, sparks his heightened threat response: he feels every touch as a potential danger and cannot let himself relax even in a safe, familiar setting. His inability to unwind forces him to avoid being around children. He refuses to let his grandchildren play on the roof, shuns family gatherings, and when his wife insists they stay in town, he chooses to work late into the night, keeping his body busy to block the intrusive images. He believes that by keeping himself busy, he can keep the terror at bay, yet every idle moment brings the memory home again. For months, the pattern hardened into habit. The work he once loved became a refuge and a prison. Mahmoud stopped attending his son's football games, and his wife expressed worry about the growing distance between them. He stopped checking the local news, but when he did, the anxiety swelled, forcing him to withdraw further. The sleepless nights and the constant startle attacks made him dread the next day, and the avoidance of triggers seemed like the only way to keep the threat from erupting again. Yet this avoidance only deepened the isolation, leaving Mahmoud feeling trapped in a world where every familiar sound and sight could bring the old terror rushing back. Recently, a sudden fall during a routine roof inspection left him with a broken ankle. The physical pain and the inability to move freely forced him to stay home for weeks, and the absence of his usual busy schedule gave the memories a chance to surface unchecked. The relentless intrusions and the sleepless nights finally drove Mahmoud to seek help. He is terrified of losing the last thread that keeps him anchored: the sense that he can still protect his family and keep his home safe. Yet he also hopes that, with professional support, he can learn to break the loop and reclaim his life, so that his children can again play under his roof without his heart racing at every footfall.
